blocks.h: Bob, who could not find his way
items: Bob is smart, funny and the life of every party. But he keeps getting lost, even on the way to the grocery store in his own town.
One morning he falls. A brain scan finds a lump the size of a lime, right in the middle.
It sits next to the brain's place patch: a part that answers to places.
Bob draws a bicycle well. He cannot draw the plan of his own home.
Surgery goes well and Bob is back at work in days. His sense of direction does not come back. He uses his phone map.
blocks.end: One part stopped. Everything else kept working. That is how we know the brain is built from parts.

items: The brain has parts
It is not one big lump. Different parts do different jobs.
Some parts are very specific
One part for faces, one for places. Lose one, keep the rest.
Brain parts match the mind
Each part tells us about one piece of how we think.
Brains change
They change as we grow and learn. Young brains recover best.
Your brain is you
Doctors move hearts. Never brains: you would become someone else.
Many ways to look
Scientists use tests, scans and patients like Bob, all together.
Tests
Show a picture, ask what you see, time the answer.
Brain photos
MRI: a picture of the inside of the head.
Brain movies
fMRI: which parts work harder while you think.
People like Bob
What still works, and what stops, after a part is hurt.
Brain waves
EEG and MEG: tiny signals read from outside the head.
Wiring maps
Pictures of the cables that link the parts.

blocks.text: A computer can name the cat in a photo. It still cannot get the joke in a photo. Your brain can.

items: Seeing map
The back of the brain holds a map of what you see. Scientists showed people a letter M and saw an M light up there.
Touch map
A strip on top maps your whole body. Fingertips and lips get the biggest patches.
Sound map
Above the ear, low and high notes sit in order, like keys on a piano.
H.M. had both memory curls removed. From then on he could not keep any new memory.
Lonni Sue, an artist and pilot, lost her memory parts to a virus. She is smart, funny and still paints, but remembers no event of her life.
S.M. has no fear almonds. She feels no fear and trusts everyone, even when she should not.
A boy born without a cerebellum learned to walk late, then did almost everything well.
A woman who lost her motion area saw the world in still frames. Pouring water, the cup overflowed before she noticed.
blocks.end: Each part has its own job. Lose one, and only that job goes.

It looks white both times, though the light reaching your eye changed. Your brain takes the colour of the light away.

The only way to know a part is truly needed.
blocks.end: Brain waves are like a microphone on a stadium roof: you hear the goal, not the chat.

Looking at a ball, a box or a written sign, the patient sees a face appear on top.
blocks.end: Switch the face area on and you see faces. Only faces.

blocks.text: Jacob, born face-blind, has a normal-looking face area. Having the part is not enough: its links matter too.

entries.title: Testing an Idea
entries.what: A fair test changes one thing, measures one thing, and rules out every other explanation.
entries.gives: You can design your own fair test and spot weak claims.
entries.pic: Two boxes that differ in only one thing: a snake and a coiled garden hose.

steps.t: Pick a question, for example: does music help me remember words?
Write the one thing you change (music on or off) and the one thing you measure (words remembered).
List three other differences that could sneak in: time of day, tiredness, the word list. Keep them equal.
Do both versions yourself, in mixed order, over four days.
Compare the averages. Only one thing differed, so only it can explain the gap.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 6: Experimental Design

words.meaning: A hidden second difference between your two conditions that could explain the result.
A condition just like the test one, minus the key thing.
A magnetic coil on the scalp that briefly scrambles the brain area underneath.

blocks.k: Words that keep a test fair
blocks.h: Six tools of a good design
items: Change
The one thing you vary on purpose.
Measure
The one thing you count or time.
Prediction
Exactly what you will see if your idea is right.
Hidden difference
Faces are also curvier and more interesting than objects. That could be the real cause.
Control
Snakes versus worms or garden hoses: same shape, no snake.
Baseline
As close to "off" as possible: staring at a dot.

blocks.h: To prove a cause, change the cause
items: A scan shows a part turning on. It does not show the part is needed.
TMS: a coil on the scalp sends a pulse shorter than a thousandth of a second.
Over a face area near the scalp, it drops a face-matching score from 85% to 78%.
It only works 60 to 100 thousandths of a second after the face appears.
Monkeys have six face patches wired to each other, like one team.
blocks.end: TMS is not used on people prone to seizures.

blocks.text: Coffee raises the brain-scan signal. One lab hands volunteers chocolate espresso beans before a scan.

entries.title: Faces, Places and Bodies
entries.what: Only a few things get their own patch in everyone's brain: faces, places, bodies and written words.
entries.gives: You see which kinds of seeing the brain treats as special.
entries.pic: The underside of a brain with three patches: a face, a house and a body.

steps.t: Find a busy photo: a crowd or a street.
Look for 3 seconds, then close your eyes.
Say everything you remember.
People, faces and the shape of the place come first. Each has its own brain team.
Now name three objects from the photo.
Objects come slower. No single patch handles cars or chairs.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 7: Category Selectivity, Controversies, and MVPA

words.meaning: A kind of thing: faces, places, bodies, cars.
Guessing what someone saw from the pattern in their brain scan.
A patch under the brain that answers most to faces.

items: Faces
Own patch in everyone
Places
Own patch in everyone
Bodies
Own patch in everyone
Written words
Own patch once you can read
Snakes and spiders
No patch found
Food, flowers, cars, chairs
No patch found

blocks.h: Does the face area know chairs?
items: The challenge
Even a weak answer can carry a pattern that tells chairs from cars.
The finding
It does, a little.
The reply
You can use a vending machine as a clock. That is not its job.

blocks.h: Can a scan read your mind?
items: Scan a person looking at shoes, then cats. Store each pattern.
Show a new picture. Which stored pattern does it match?
It works a little.
Easy to block: move your head, move your tongue, or do sums in your head.
In a monkey, 167 single cells tell five faces apart. A scan of the same spot cannot.
blocks.end: Each scan pixel averages hundreds of thousands of cells.

blocks.text: Watch flashing letters instead of the face on screen, and your face area answers less. What you choose to notice changes your brain.

entries.title: Finding Your Way
entries.what: To travel, your brain answers two questions: where am I, and how do I get there?
entries.gives: You know which brain parts keep you oriented, and why some people get lost.
entries.pic: A map pin, a compass arrow and a path bending around a wall.

steps.t: Stand still in a room you know.
Close your eyes. Point to the door, the window and the far wall.
Say roughly how far away each one is.
Open your eyes and check. You carry the shape of the room with you.
Walk a new route once, then draw it from memory.
See which turns and landmarks stayed with you.

entries.safety: Stand still with your eyes closed; never walk with your eyes shut.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 8: Navigation I

words.meaning: Heading straight for something you can see or hear.
The map of a place you carry in your head.
A patch under the brain that answers to the shape of the space around you.

items: A monarch butterfly weighs half a gram and flies over 2,000 miles to a few acres of forest in Mexico.
The round trip takes four generations. Great-great-grandchildren find the same trees.
A loggerhead turtle returns after 20 years to the beach where she hatched.
Bats keep their sense of direction while flying upside down in the dark.
A desert ant wanders far, finds food, and runs in a straight line home. Carried elsewhere, it runs the same line.
blocks.end: The ant counts its own steps and turns, with no landmarks at all.

items: Where am I
A place you know, or at least the kind of place.
The shape of space
Walls, doors and how far each one is.
Which way I face
Out of the subway in Manhattan, you know the corner but not north from south.
An inner map
Rats trained on a twisting route chose the direct path when a new one opened.
A way back
A way to reset when you get lost.
Paths and walls
Where you can actually walk: glass lets you see through, not walk through.

Strong

blocks.end: It cares about the shape of space, not the things in it.

blocks.text: A patient with a tiny current on his place area said he saw a train station, a staircase, and a closet stuffed with blue things.

entries.title: Your Inner Map
entries.what: Special cells mark where you are, which way you face and how far you have moved.
entries.gives: You see how the brain keeps a living map, and why it sometimes flips.
entries.pic: A grid of dots in hexagons, a compass needle and one bronze spot: grid, direction and place cells.

steps.t: Sit on a swivel chair with your eyes closed. A friend turns you slowly, then stops.
Point to the door.
Your inner compass still has a guess, using your balance sense.
Eyes open: walk 10 steps, turn left, walk 5 steps.
Point back to where you started without looking.
Direction and distance cells added up your path, like the desert ant.

entries.safety: Stop if you feel dizzy; keep a friend beside you while your eyes are closed.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 9: Navigation II

words.meaning: A cell that fires only when you are in one spot.
A cell that fires at many spots laid out like a honeycomb. It measures distance.
A curled part deep inside that holds your inner map and new memories.

items: Place cells
Each fires in one spot of the room, whichever way you face.
Direction cells
Each fires when you face one way. Together: a compass.
Grid cells
Fire at points on a honeycomb across the floor. They measure how far you went.
blocks.end: Border cells add the walls and cliff edges. In 2014 the discoverers of place and grid cells shared a Nobel Prize.

items: A rat sees food hidden in one corner of a long room, then gets turned around.
It searches the right corner and the opposite one equally. Same shape, same guess.
One bright wall would solve it. The rat ignores it.
Toddlers do the same, even with a red velvet wall that plays music.
Adults do the same while busy repeating radio speech out loud.
blocks.end: Colours change with the seasons; the shape of the land stays.

items: Made-up birds
Learning birds by neck and leg length makes a grid pattern.
Other people
Power and friendship form a map. Bats track where another bat is.
Deciding
At a junction, a rat's place cells run ahead down both paths first.

blocks.text: That sudden "wait, I am facing the wrong way" moment is real: all your place cells flip together.

entries.title: Born or Learned?
entries.what: Some face skills appear in the first days of life; experience then tunes and narrows them.
entries.gives: You see nature and nurture as a team, not a fight.
entries.pic: A baby's face turning to follow a simple face drawing on a paddle.

steps.t: Find photos of two monkeys and two human strangers.
Show a friend one monkey face, then both, and ask which one they saw.
Do the same with the human faces.
Humans are easy and monkeys are hard. At six months, you could tell monkey faces apart too.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 10: Development, Nature and Nurture I

words.meaning: Getting bored of something seen again and again, so you look away sooner.
Losing skills you never use, such as telling monkey faces apart.
The fatty wrap on nerve fibres that makes signals travel faster.

So a baby can tell us what looks "same" and what looks "new".
blocks.end: Babies cannot talk, but their eyes can answer.

items: Faces of other species
Clear at six months, gone by nine.
Sounds of other languages
Babies hear all the world's speech sounds. Adults hear their own.
How to keep it
Naming photos, "Monkey Joe, Monkey Bob", from 6 to 12 months keeps the skill. Just "look!" does not.
blocks.end: Faces of other groups work the same way. Moving before about age 12 fixes it.

blocks.text: Monkeys raised by keepers in welder's masks never saw a face. At first sight they still preferred faces and told them apart.

entries.title: How Brains Grow
entries.what: What flows into a brain area, and how it is wired, shapes what that area becomes.
entries.gives: You see what experience can change, and what stays fixed.
entries.pic: Fibres running into a patch of brain, one bronze lead ending at the reading spot.

steps.t: Pick a script you cannot read: Hebrew, Chinese or Arabic.
Look at one line for 10 seconds, then copy it from memory.
Do the same with a line of English.
English comes out whole; the other comes out in pieces. Your reading area knows your letters, and it only learned them after school began.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 11: Development, Nature and Nurture II

words.meaning: A picture of the brain's long fibres, made by following water along them.
A small patch on the left underside of the brain that learns letters.
An early time when the brain can change most.

blocks.h: Ferrets that hear with their eyes
items: Ferrets are born very early, eyes still closed.
At birth, signals from the eyes were rerouted into the hearing cortex.
The hearing cortex grew the striped layout normally found in seeing cortex.
Trained to press one button for light and another for sound, the ferret pressed "light".
It saw with its hearing cortex.
blocks.end: What flows in shapes the area.

items: Too new to be built in
People have written for only a few thousand years.
Learned at school
Not active at age 5, active at 8, in the same children.
Your scripts only
It answers to Hebrew only in people who read Hebrew.
blocks.end: Its future spot can be read from the brain's wiring at age 5.

items: Adult stroke
Language rarely comes back fully.
Damage in the first months
Language moves to the right side and works well.
Stroke on day one
One boy saw objects well but never knew a face.
Born blind
The seeing cortex takes on language.
Born blind, hearing faces
Laughing and chewing sounds still reach the usual face spot.
Brain-training apps
You improve at the game, not in general.

blocks.text: Nerve fibres are wrapped in fat, so water slides along them, not across. Scanners follow the water to draw the brain's wiring.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.what: You sense "about how many" at a glance, without counting, and so do babies and many animals.
entries.gives: You see where your feel for numbers comes from, and why it matters for maths.
entries.pic: Two clouds of dots: the bronze cloud has twice as many.

steps.t: Grab two handfuls of dried beans or coins.
Spill them in two piles. Without counting, say which is bigger.
Repeat with piles closer in size.
Easy when one pile is double, hard when they are close. Your number sense works by ratio.
Count both piles to check.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 13: Number

words.meaning: Knowing roughly how many without counting.
Telling two amounts apart depends on their ratio, not their difference.
A lifelong weak number sense, unrelated to how clever someone is.

Fish join the bigger school: more fish, less chance of being eaten.
Lions weigh how many rivals there are before they fight.
Male Túngara frogs each add one more note to a rival's call.
Rats trained on 2 or 4 flashes, given 2 flashes plus 2 tones, press the "4" lever.
Bees learn: blue means add one, yellow means take one away.
blocks.end: Bees even treat a blank card as less than one.

items: By ratio
The same rule judges brightness, weight and loudness.
Across the senses
Dots against beeps is almost as easy as dots against dots.
An inner number line
Is 63 bigger than 65? You slow down near the target.
blocks.end: A groove near the top-back of the brain holds cells tuned to "two" or "six".

blocks.text: Kindergarten speed at "how many dots?" predicts arithmetic four years later, but not reading or general puzzles.

entries.title: Hearing Speech
entries.what: From waves of air, your brain works out where a sound is, what made it, what is said and who said it.
entries.gives: You see the steps from your ear to understanding a voice.
entries.pic: Sound waves entering an ear and curling into the snail-shaped cochlea.

steps.t: Sit with your eyes closed while a friend moves around the room, talking.
Point to the voice each time it moves.
You find it without looking.
Ask your friend to drop a spoon, a pencil and a plastic cup on the table.
You hear what each is made of.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 15: Hearing and Speech

words.meaning: The snail-shaped part of the inner ear that sorts sound by pitch.
A picture of sound: pitch going up, time going across.
The smallest sound that changes a word, like b and p in bat and pat.

items: The scene
What kind of room, what is happening.
Where
Eyes closed, you still know.
What made it
A door, a dog, a kettle.
What it is made of
Wood, plastic, metal.
What is said
The words.
Who said it
A friend, a stranger, young or old.

blocks.end: Seeing has one stop on the way; hearing has many.

items: Same word, new voice
Every speaker makes a word look different on a sound picture.
Sounds pile up
Music and talk arrive mixed. Like x + y = 9: solve for both.
Echoes
Sound bounces off walls and smears, yet tells you how big the room is.
blocks.end: Bat and pat differ by one tiny delay: about 65 thousandths of a second.

blocks.text: Your speech area answers just as strongly to a language you do not understand. It handles speech sounds, not meaning.

entries.title: Music
entries.what: Music is found in every human culture and has its own patch of brain, separate from language.
entries.gives: You see why music is part of being human, not a frill.
entries.pic: A bone flute, a beat line and two notes: melody and rhythm.

steps.t: Pick a song everyone knows.
Hum it starting low, then starting high.
Still the same song: you hear the steps between notes, not the exact notes. No animal does this.
Clap a steady beat with a friend. Then one of you skips a clap.
You both feel the gap. So do sleeping two-day-old babies.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 16: Music

words.meaning: Knowing a tune by its steps, whatever note it starts on.
Trouble hearing tunes, from birth or after brain damage.
Notes that sound smooth together. Liking it is learned.

To charm a mate
Darwin thought our ancestors sang before they spoke.
To comfort a baby
Song tells a baby you are there while your hands are busy.
A happy side effect
"Auditory cheesecake": built from skills meant for other jobs.
Language areas ignore music. Music areas ignore sentences.
Scanning people on 165 everyday sounds, a computer found a speech pattern and a separate music pattern.
The music pattern is there even in people who never took a lesson.
Some single spots in the brain answer only to song.
In a remote Bolivian village, people do not prefer "nice" chords over clashing ones. That taste is learned.
blocks.end: People born tone deaf also miss whether a sentence is a question.

blocks.text: At five months, babies know a tune you taught them, even when you sing it higher or lower.

entries.title: Language
entries.what: Language turns an idea in one head into the same idea in another, and it is separate from thinking itself.
entries.gives: You see what words add to thought, and what thought does without them.
entries.pic: Two heads joined by a line of sound waves, with the same bronze idea in each.

steps.t: Find a friend.
Say "shark bites man", then "man bites shark".
Same words, new meaning. Word order carries it.
Close your eyes and point south. Open them and check.
Speakers of some Aboriginal languages always know, because their language asks for it in every sentence.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 18: Language I

words.meaning: The rules for putting words in order.
Losing language after brain damage.
What someone really means, beyond the exact words.

items: Sounds and words
Sounds, or hand shapes in sign languages, and what each word stands for.
Grammar
"Shark bites man" is not "man bites shark".
Real intent
"It would be great if you passed the salt" means: pass the salt.
Babies of three to six months think richly with no words yet.
The Pirahã of the Amazon have no number words, yet match amounts by eye.
In 1861 a patient called Tan could say only "tan", yet still thought clearly.
People who lose almost all language to a stroke still do sums, logic and puzzles, and enjoy music.
An art critic losing words to a tumour wrote that his thoughts stayed vast and normal.
blocks.end: Language is not thought. But children need it to learn.

items: 1,000 names
She knows a name for each toy.
New word, new toy
Told to find "Darwin", she picks the one toy she does not know.
No grammar
She cannot follow who did what to whom.
blocks.end: People combine words to say things nobody has ever said before.

blocks.text: Some Australian speakers greet you with "which way are you going?" and warn you of a bug on your southeast leg.

entries.title: Other Minds
entries.what: You read what others see, want and believe, and one small brain area works on beliefs alone.
entries.gives: You see how we understand each other, and why it takes years to grow.
entries.pic: Two figures: one looks at a box, the other holds a bronze thought bubble with the box inside.

steps.t: Take two cups, a coin and a small toy figure.
While the figure "watches", hide the coin under cup A.
Move the figure away. Now move the coin to cup B.
Ask a child aged 3 to 7: where will the figure look?
Five-year-olds say A: the figure did not see the move. Three-year-olds say B.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 20: Mentalizing and Theory of Mind

words.meaning: Understanding that others have their own thoughts and beliefs.
Someone believing something that is no longer true.
A spot above and behind the right ear that works on other people's thoughts.

items: Ivan puts his cheese sandwich on a chest and goes for a drink.
The wind blows it onto the grass. Joshua puts his own sandwich on the chest.
A five-year-old says: Ivan will not know which one is his.
A three-year-old says Ivan will take his own, then explains: his was dirty.
Only around seven do children say the wind should get in trouble.
blocks.end: Knowing that others can believe wrong things takes years.

items: What they see
What reached their eyes and what did not.
What they want
Romeo reaches for the bottle because he wants to die.
What they believe
He believes Juliet is dead. She is not.
Someone's thoughts
Strong
Someone's looks
Quiet
Someone's hunger or pain
Quiet
A wordless cartoon
Strong at the thinking moments
Children
Keeps sharpening after age four
Zapped with TMS
Accidents get judged more harshly
blocks.end: Poison labelled "sugar" or labelled "toxic": what Grace believed changes how we judge her.

blocks.text: Toddlers of 18 months help a stranger whose hands are full, without being asked.

entries.title: Brain Teams
entries.what: Brain areas work in networks, linked by long fibres, and the teams stay in step even at rest.
entries.gives: You see how parts join forces, and which team keeps you clever on new problems.
entries.pic: Three bronze dots linked by curved fibres, and two grey dots linked to each other.

steps.t: Lie down for five minutes with your eyes closed and no task.
Notice where your thoughts go.
Daydreams, plans and other people: your resting team at work.
Now work out 17 × 13 in your head.
Feel the switch: the hard-task team takes over.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 21: Brain Networks

words.meaning: The brain's cables: long fibres wrapped in fat.
Areas busy when you rest and let your mind wander.
Areas that switch on for any difficult problem.

items: of the human brain is wiring (mice: 10%)
around the Earth, laid end to end
of fibres lost each decade after age 20
Resting team
Busy when nobody gives you a task.
Hard-task team
Switches on for any difficult puzzle: memory, maths, fine judgments.
Language team
Its parts rise and fall together even 10-12 cm apart, and apart from the hard-task team.

blocks.h: Cables decide what a part can do
items: What flows into a part decides what it can know.
Where its fibres go decides what it can change.
Children with dyslexia have a less orderly cable between two language areas.
Brains keep wires short, like a good circuit board: wire costs fuel and space.
Damage to the hard-task team lowers IQ in step with tissue lost; damage elsewhere does not.
blocks.end: The hard-task team is the brain's general problem-solver.

blocks.text: Scans of the wiring need no task at all. People often fall asleep while the machine maps their cables.

entries.title: Attention and Awareness
entries.what: Attention lets a small part of what reaches your senses into awareness and filters out the rest.
entries.gives: You see how much you miss, and how to choose what you notice.
entries.pic: An eye with a bronze beam lighting one shape among many grey ones.

steps.t: Find a "spot the difference" pair of pictures.
Flip between them once a second without searching.
Changes hide in plain sight.
Now search one small area at a time.
They appear. You see what you attend to.
Look at a friend's nose while they hold up fingers to the side. Count them without moving your eyes.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 24: Attention and Awareness

words.meaning: The filter that picks what you process.
Missing big changes right in front of you.
What you actually experience seeing or hearing.

blocks.h: How much we do not see
items: A street photo flashes again and again. Awnings, colours and a car change. Most people miss most of it.
In a short murder-mystery film, the whole set changes between shots. Viewers notice almost nothing.
Trained pilots landing in a fog simulator: many flew straight through a plane parked on the runway.
Afterwards they could not believe it.
A hands-free phone still splits a limited mind while you drive.
blocks.end: Attention is a filter: limited, and chosen.

items: Moving the eyes
Two to four jumps a second. The sharp centre of gaze gets a huge share of seeing cortex.
Without moving
Eyes on a nose, you can still count fingers to one side.
Picking targets
Red letters among the blue ones cost you nothing: attention chooses what counts.
Turns areas up
The face area answers far more when you watch faces.
Starts early
Even the first relay after the eye is filtered.
A control team
Front and top-back areas aim the filter.
When it breaks
After damage on both sides, people see one object at a time.
Flipping pictures
A face to one eye, a house to the other: awareness flips, the eyes do not.
Seen but unseen
A missed scene still nudges the place area a little.

blocks.text: A pike catches its first fish faster when there is one stickleback in the tank than when there are ten.

entries.title: The Blind Spot
entries.what: Each eye has a spot with no light cells, where the nerve leaves the eye. The brain fills the hole in.
entries.gives: What you see is part seeing and part filling in. Knowing this keeps you curious about what is really there.
entries.pic: A cross and a dot. At the right distance the dot (bronze) vanishes.

steps.t: On paper, draw a small cross on the left and a dot 8 cm to the right.
Hold the paper at arm's length. Close your left eye.
Look only at the cross with your right eye.
Slowly bring the paper closer.
At one distance the dot disappears and the paper looks whole. Your brain filled the gap.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · The eye and the visual system

words.meaning: The thin layer at the back of the eye that catches light.
The brain guessing what belongs in a gap so you see a whole picture.

entries.title: The NLP Communication Model
entries.what: NLP is a set of simple tools for changing how you think, feel and act.
entries.gives: You can change a reaction step by step, instead of only talking about it.
entries.pic: A funnel: lots of information goes into your mind, only a little gets through.

steps.t: Notice that your mind cannot take in everything around you.
It keeps a little, leaves a lot out, and fills the gaps with guesses.
So the world in your head is your own picture of it, not the world itself.
Listen to the words you use. They show your picture.
Choose one reaction you want to change.
Change one small thing, and see if the reaction changes.

source.name: Richard Bandler & John Grinder, UC Santa Cruz, 1970s

words.meaning: The version of the world you carry in your head. Like a map of a city: useful, but not the city itself.
How your mind copes: it keeps some things and drops others. Like hearing only your name in a noisy room.

entries.title: The Presuppositions of NLP
entries.what: The basic working beliefs of NLP. You act as if they are true because they are useful.
entries.gives: They set the attitude for every technique that follows.
entries.pic: A house on a foundation: the beliefs everything else is built on.

steps.t: Learn the main presuppositions, one at a time.
The map is not the territory: your picture of the world is not the world itself.
There is no failure, only feedback: every result teaches you something.
The meaning of communication is the response you get: judge your message by how it lands.
Every behaviour has a positive intention: behind every action is a good reason.
People already have the resources they need, or can build them.
If one thing does not work, do something different.
Choose one presupposition each week and act as if it is true.

words.meaning: Something you take as true in order to start, like the rules of a game.
Information about what happened, used to do better next time.

entries.title: Calibration
entries.what: Noticing small changes in a person's face, skin and breathing.
entries.gives: You see how a person feels, often before they say it.
entries.pic: An eye watching closely for small changes.

steps.t: Watch the person when they are calm. This is their normal.
Choose one thing to watch: breathing, skin colour or lips.
Talk about something they like.
Then talk about something they dislike.
Notice what changes compared with their normal.
Do not guess what it means. Only notice the change.
Practise one signal a day for a week.

entries.time: 1 week, a few minutes a day

words.meaning: How a person looks when they are calm and normal.
Learning one person's own signals by watching closely.

entries.title: Representational Systems (VAKOG)
entries.what: The five senses the mind uses to build inner experience: seeing, hearing, feeling, smelling and tasting.
entries.gives: You learn how you and others store and recall experience.
entries.pic: Symbols for the five senses: eye, sound, hand, nose and mouth.

steps.t: Learn the letters: V visual (seeing), A auditory (hearing), K kinaesthetic (feeling), O olfactory (smell), G gustatory (taste).
Remember your last holiday.
Notice what comes first: a picture, a sound or a feeling.
Notice which senses are strong and which are faint.
Ask a friend the same question and compare.
Remember: everyone uses all the senses; one may lead in a given moment.

words.meaning: Visual, Auditory, Kinaesthetic, Olfactory, Gustatory: seeing, hearing, feeling, smell, taste.
The sense that brings a memory up first.

entries.title: Sensory Predicates & Translation
entries.what: Listening for seeing, hearing and feeling words, and saying an idea in each of them.
entries.gives: Your message reaches more people, more easily.
entries.pic: An eye, sound waves and a hand: one idea, said three ways.

steps.t: Seeing words: see, clear, look, picture.
Hearing words: sounds, hear, rings a bell.
Feeling words: feel, grasp, solid. Thinking words: makes sense, consider.
Notice which kind a person uses most right now.
Answer with the same kind of words.
Translate: 'I see what you mean' → 'That sounds right' → 'That feels right' → 'That makes sense.'
When you explain something important, say it once in each sense.

words.meaning: A sensory word, such as 'see', 'hear' or 'feel', that shows which sense a person is using.
Self-talk and logic words, such as 'makes sense'.

entries.title: Eye Accessing Cues
entries.what: An old NLP idea that the direction of the eyes shows how a person is thinking.
entries.gives: Tests showed it does not work. It is listed so you know.
entries.pic: Arrows for eye directions, crossed out: the idea did not pass the tests.

steps.t: The idea: eyes up means pictures, sideways means sounds, down means feelings.
Researchers tested it carefully.
A 2012 study found no link with thinking style or lying.
Never judge a person by where they look.
Instead, watch for changes against their normal, as in Calibration.

words.meaning: The idea that eye movements show which sense you are using. Not supported by research.

entries.title: Synesthesia & Overlap
entries.what: How one sense can trigger another, like a smell bringing back a picture.
entries.gives: When one sense is weak, you can reach it through a stronger one.
entries.pic: Two senses linked by an arrow: a smell leading to a picture.

steps.t: Think of a smell you love, such as fresh bread.
Notice the picture that comes with it.
Notice the feeling that follows.
If a picture is hard to see, start with a sound or a feeling instead.
Let it lead you, step by step, into the other senses.
Notice which links are strongest for you.

words.meaning: In NLP: one sense automatically triggering another, such as a sound bringing a feeling.
Using a strong sense to open a weaker one.

entries.title: Association & Dissociation
entries.what: Seeing a memory through your own eyes, or watching yourself from outside.
entries.gives: Inside makes a feeling stronger. Outside makes it smaller.
entries.pic: An eye watching a screen: you watching yourself in a memory.

steps.t: Remember a happy moment, through your own eyes.
Notice how strong the feeling is.
Now see yourself in that memory, as if on a screen.
Notice the feeling gets smaller.
Do the same with a mildly unpleasant memory, from outside.
Make that picture smaller and further away.
The rule: step into good memories. Step out of bad ones.

entries.safety: For painful memories or trauma, work with a qualified clinician.

source.name: NLP · Ethan Kross & Özlem Ayduk, self-distancing research

words.meaning: Looking out through your own eyes, as if you are there again.
Watching yourself in the memory, like watching a film.

entries.title: Uptime & Downtime
entries.what: Two modes of attention: outward to the world (uptime) or inward to your thoughts (downtime).
entries.gives: You can choose where your attention goes, on purpose.
entries.pic: An eye looking out, and an eye looking inward.

steps.t: Sit and notice where your attention is right now.
Uptime: put all your attention outside: what you see, hear and feel on your skin.
Stay there for one minute, without inner talk.
Downtime: close your eyes and turn your attention to your thoughts and inner pictures.
Stay there for one minute.
Switch between the two, faster each time.
Use uptime when you listen to people; use downtime when you plan or imagine.

words.meaning: All attention on the outside world, here and now.
Attention on your inner world: thoughts, memories, pictures.

entries.title: Physiological Matching & Mirroring
entries.what: Gently copying a person's posture, speed and tone so they feel at ease with you.
entries.gives: People trust those who feel similar to them.
entries.pic: Two people standing the same way.

steps.t: Notice how they sit, move, breathe and speak.
Copy one or two things, gently and naturally.
Speak at their speed and volume.
Use some of their words.
Do this for a few minutes. This is called pacing.
Test: change your posture and see if they follow.
If they follow, you can lead. If not, keep pacing.

entries.time: A few minutes in any conversation

source.name: Bandler & Grinder · Chartrand & Bargh 1999, the chameleon effect

words.meaning: A feeling of trust and ease between two people.
Meeting a person where they are before you guide them anywhere.

entries.title: Cross-Over Mirroring
entries.what: Matching one of a person's rhythms with a different part of your body.
entries.gives: You build rapport without copying them openly.
entries.pic: A breathing wave, matched by small taps.

steps.t: Notice one rhythm in the person: breathing, blinking or nodding.
Choose a different, small movement of your own: a finger, a foot or your voice.
Match their rhythm with it. Example: tap a finger each time they breathe out.
Keep it small and natural.
Notice if they feel more at ease.

words.meaning: Matching one behaviour with a different one, such as breathing with a hand movement.

entries.title: Vocal Pacing
entries.what: Matching how a person speaks: tone, speed, volume and pauses.
entries.gives: People feel understood when your voice sounds like theirs.
entries.pic: Two sound waves with the same shape.

steps.t: Listen to the person's voice: fast or slow, loud or soft, high or low.
Match their speed.
Match their volume.
Match their pauses and rhythm.
Keep your own natural voice; only adjust it.
Notice whether the talk flows more easily.

words.meaning: How the voice sounds: pitch, warmth and rhythm.
Speed of speech.

entries.title: Verbal Pacing & Backtracking
entries.what: Repeating what someone said, using their own important words.
entries.gives: They feel heard, and mistakes show up early.
entries.pic: A speech bubble with an arrow back: you give their words back to them.

steps.t: Listen for the important words they use.
Remember them.
Repeat the main point using their words, not yours.
Keep it short.
Ask: 'Did I get that right?'
Correct it if needed, then continue.

words.meaning: A short summary in the other person's own words.

entries.title: Pacing & Leading
entries.what: First meeting a person where they are, then guiding them somewhere new.
entries.gives: People follow you when they feel you understand them first.
entries.pic: Two people walking side by side, then one leading.

steps.t: Pace: say or do things that are plainly true for them now.
Example: 'You've had a long day, you're here, and you want this sorted.'
Match their posture and voice at the same time.
Pace three or four times.
Lead: make one small change, in words or posture.
Notice if they follow. If not, pace more.

words.meaning: Matching what is true for the person right now.
Guiding gently in a new direction after pacing.

entries.title: Breaking Rapport
entries.what: Breaking the connection on purpose, to stop a mood or end a talk politely.
entries.gives: You can end a conversation kindly, without being rude.
entries.pic: Two people, one turning away.

steps.t: Decide the talk should end or the mood should change.
Turn your body slightly away.
Change your speed or volume.
Look away for a moment.
End with a warm, clear sentence.

words.meaning: Doing the opposite of the other person, on purpose.

entries.title: Present State & Desired State
entries.what: Every change has the same shape: where you are, where you want to be, and what gets you there.
entries.gives: You always know where to start.
entries.pic: Grey circle: where you are now. Bronze circle: where you want to be. The arrow: the help you need.

steps.t: Describe where you are now: what you see, hear and feel.
Describe where you want to be, the same way.
Name what is missing between the two.
Choose one tool from this section that adds what is missing.
Use the tool.
Check: are you closer to where you want to be?

words.meaning: How things are now.
How you want things to be.

entries.title: The Well-Formed Outcome Checklist
entries.what: A checklist that turns a wish into a clear goal.
entries.gives: A clear goal is much easier to reach than a vague wish.
entries.pic: A target: a goal you can see clearly is a goal you can hit.

steps.t: Say what you want, not what you don't want: 'I want calm', not 'I don't want stress'.
Picture it done: what do you see, hear and feel?
Decide how you will know you have it.
Check that it is up to you, not someone else.
Decide where, when and with whom.
List what you already have and what you still need.
Ask: what will I gain, and what will I give up?
Take the first small step today.

source.name: NLP well-formed outcome conditions, Bandler & Grinder

words.meaning: The result you want.
The sign that shows you got it. For example: 'I sleep eight hours a night.'

entries.title: Evidence Procedures
entries.what: Deciding exactly what you will see, hear and feel when a goal is reached.
entries.gives: You know for certain when you have arrived.
entries.pic: A checklist with an eye, an ear and a hand.

steps.t: Take one goal.
Ask: 'What will I see when I have it?'
Ask: 'What will I hear?'
Ask: 'What will I feel?'
Make each sign specific and measurable.
Write the evidence down, and check it regularly.

words.meaning: The exact signs that prove a goal is reached.

entries.title: Ecology Check
entries.what: Checking that a change is good for your whole life, not just one part of it.
entries.gives: A change that hurts another part of your life does not last.
entries.pic: You in the centre, connected to the people and parts of your life around you.

steps.t: Name the change you want.
Ask: what will I gain if I get it?
Ask: what will I lose if I get it?
Ask: what happens if I don't get it?
Think about family, work, health and money.
Adjust the change until every answer feels right.

words.meaning: Here it means: is this change good for me, for the people around me, and for my life as a whole?

entries.title: The Disney Creativity Strategy
entries.what: Three roles for creative work: dreamer, planner and critic.
entries.gives: Each role works better on its own.
entries.pic: Three circles: Dreamer, Realist, Critic.

steps.t: Choose three places in the room.
Place 1, Dreamer: imagine the idea with no limits.
Place 2, Realist: plan how it would work in practice, step by step.
Place 3, Critic: find what is missing in the plan, not in the person.
Take the feedback back to the dreamer.
Repeat until all three agree.

words.meaning: The role that imagines freely, with no limits.
The role that turns the dream into a practical plan.
The role that checks the plan for gaps and risks.

entries.title: State Elicitation & Management
entries.what: Bringing back a feeling on purpose by reliving a time you had it.
entries.gives: You can choose your state instead of waiting for it.
entries.pic: A dial turned up: a feeling growing on purpose.

steps.t: Choose the state, such as confidence.
Ask: 'Can you remember a specific time you felt totally confident?'
Go back to that time: see what you saw, hear what you heard, feel what you felt.
Look through your own eyes, as if you are there.
Let the feeling grow.
Notice the signs in the body: breathing, posture, face.
Shake it off, and notice that you can return to it.

words.meaning: The whole of how you feel right now, in mind and body.
Bring out, on purpose.

entries.title: The 4 Keys to Anchoring
entries.what: The four rules that make an anchor strong.
entries.gives: When you follow them, anchors work. When you skip them, anchors fade.
entries.pic: Four keys: intensity, timing, uniqueness, replication.

steps.t: Learn the four keys before you set any anchor.
1. Intensity: the feeling must be strong.
2. Timing: set the anchor at the peak, just before the feeling starts to fade.
3. Uniqueness: use a touch you do not use every day.
4. Replication: repeat the touch exactly the same way each time.
Check every anchor against the four keys.

words.meaning: The highest point of a feeling.
Doing it exactly the same way each time.

entries.title: Basic Resource Anchoring (V-A-K)
entries.what: Linking a good feeling to a simple touch, so you can bring it back when you need it.
entries.gives: You can feel calm or confident on purpose.
entries.pic: A hand: a touch on one knuckle brings the feeling back.

steps.t: Choose one good feeling, such as calm.
Remember one moment when you felt it strongly.
Close your eyes and go back there: see, hear and feel it.
Let the feeling grow. Count from 5 up to 10.
At 10, press one knuckle for a few seconds. Then let go.
Open your eyes and look around.
You can also anchor with an image (visual) or a word said in a set tone (auditory).
Repeat 3 to 5 times.
Test: press the knuckle. Does the feeling come back?

entries.safety: Positive states only. If distress appears, stop and open your eyes.

source.name: Bandler & Grinder, after Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning

words.meaning: A trigger linked to a feeling. Like a song that always makes you happy.
How you feel right now: calm, nervous, excited.

entries.title: Stacking Anchors
entries.what: Placing several good feelings on the same touch.
entries.gives: One touch brings back a strong mix, such as calm, confident and focused.
entries.pic: Three layers on one point.

steps.t: Choose 3 to 5 good feelings, such as calm, confident and focused.
Choose one touch point, such as one knuckle.
Bring back the first feeling and anchor it at its peak.
Shake it off.
Bring back the next feeling and anchor it on the same spot.
Repeat for each feeling.
Test: press the spot and notice the combined feeling.

words.meaning: Layering several feelings on one anchor.

entries.title: Collapsing Anchors
entries.what: Using a strong good feeling to cancel a small bad one.
entries.gives: The old trigger stops upsetting you.
entries.pic: A big bronze circle swallowing a small grey one.

steps.t: Choose a small bad feeling, such as irritation, and what starts it.
Choose a strong good feeling to replace it.
Link the good feeling to one knuckle, 5 times.
Shake it off. Think of something else.
Link the bad feeling to another knuckle, once, briefly.
Shake it off again.
Press both knuckles. Let go of the bad one first.
Hold the good one until it is strong, then let go.
Test: think of the trigger. What happens now?

entries.safety: Mild states only. For anxiety, depression or trauma, work with a qualified clinician.

source.name: Bandler & Grinder · Mary Cover Jones 1924, counterconditioning

words.meaning: Here it means: two feelings meet, and the stronger one wins.

entries.title: Chaining Anchors
entries.what: A chain of feelings that takes you from stuck to moving, step by step.
entries.gives: Some jumps are too big to make in one step.
entries.pic: Dots growing one by one: small steps from stuck to strong.

steps.t: Name where you are stuck, such as putting things off, and where you want to be, such as motivated.
Choose 2 or 3 feelings in between, each a natural next step.
Make the second feeling one with drive, such as mild frustration.
Make each feeling after it good, and stronger than the last.
Link each feeling to its own knuckle.
Press the first. Add the second. Let go of the first. Continue to the end.
Always keep at least one knuckle pressed.
At the last feeling, let it grow strong, let go, and test.

entries.safety: Mild states only. For anxiety, depression or trauma, work with a qualified clinician.

words.meaning: A feeling where nothing moves, such as putting things off.

entries.title: Circle of Excellence
entries.what: An imagined circle on the floor that holds your best feeling.
entries.gives: You can step into confidence whenever you need it.
entries.pic: A circle on the floor, and you stepping in.

steps.t: Imagine a circle on the floor. Give it a colour.
Remember a time you felt very confident.
Let the feeling grow.
At its strongest, step into the circle.
Let the feeling fill you. Then step out.
Repeat 3 to 5 times.
Think of a coming moment. Step in, and take the feeling with you.

entries.safety: Positive states only. If distress appears, stop and step out.

words.meaning: Anything that helps you: a feeling, a skill, a memory.

entries.title: Future Pacing
entries.what: Practising the new you in a future situation.
entries.gives: When the real moment comes, the new reaction is ready.
entries.pic: An arrow into the future, and you standing there.

steps.t: Think of a future moment where the old reaction would show up.
Step into it in your mind.
See, hear and feel yourself reacting the new way.
Notice how others react to you.
Do the same with two more future moments.
For extra motivation: picture a big future result, then bring it closer to now.

words.meaning: Rehearsing tomorrow, today.

entries.title: Submodality Distinctions
entries.what: The small details of a picture in your mind: size, brightness, distance.
entries.gives: Change the details and the feeling changes.
entries.pic: Three sliders: brightness, size and distance.

steps.t: Think of a memory.
Notice the picture: colour, brightness, size, how near.
Notice the sound: loud or soft.
Notice the feeling: where in the body, how strong from 0 to 10.
Move the picture closer, then further away. What changes?
Step into it, then out of it. What changes?
Most often, distance and inside or outside make the biggest difference.

words.meaning: The small details of a picture, sound or feeling in your mind, like brightness or volume.

entries.title: Critical Submodality Drivers
entries.what: The one or two details of a mind picture that change the feeling the most.
entries.gives: You change the feeling quickly by changing only that detail.
entries.pic: Many sliders, with one marked in bronze: the driver.

steps.t: Think of a memory with a strong feeling.
Change one detail at a time: brightness, size, distance, colour, sound.
After each change, rate the feeling from 0 to 10.
Put each detail back before testing the next one.
Find the one or two that change the feeling most.
Those are the drivers for this memory. Use them in other techniques.

words.meaning: The detail with the biggest effect on the feeling, often distance or size.

entries.title: Contrastive Analysis
entries.what: Comparing the mind picture of a limiting experience with a helpful one.
entries.gives: The differences show exactly what to change.
entries.pic: Two pictures side by side: the second is closer, larger and brighter.

steps.t: Choose a limiting experience, such as doubt.
Choose a helpful one, such as certainty.
Note the details of the first: place, size, brightness, sound, feeling.
Note the same details of the second.
List the differences.
These differences are what you change in Belief Change and similar techniques.

words.meaning: Finding differences by comparing two things.

entries.title: The Swish Pattern
entries.what: Swapping the picture that starts a habit for a picture of your best self.
entries.gives: The old trigger starts to lead to a new reaction.
entries.pic: A big old picture, and a small new one that grows to replace it.

steps.t: Choose a small habit to change.
Find the trigger: what you see just before the habit starts.
Picture yourself at your best, seen from outside.
Put the trigger picture big and bright in front of you.
Put your best-self picture small and dark in one corner.
In one second, shrink the old one and make the new one big and bright. Say 'swish'.
Clear the screen. Never swap back.
Repeat 5 to 10 times, faster each time.
Test: think of the trigger. Where does your mind go now?

entries.safety: Mild habits only. Never for self-harm or addiction.

words.meaning: What starts a habit, such as seeing your phone.
A very fast swap of two pictures.

entries.title: Like-to-Dislike / Compulsion Blowout
entries.what: Making a food you overeat feel like a food you dislike.
entries.gives: It weakens the pull of one specific food.
entries.pic: A plate you like, an arrow, and a plate crossed out.

steps.t: Be sure you really want this change.
Choose one food you overeat, such as one brand of chocolate.
Choose a similar food you strongly dislike.
Picture the food you like. Notice where it is, how big and how bright.
Clear the screen. Do the same for the food you dislike.
Clear the screen. Give the liked food the same place, size and look as the disliked one.
Lock it in with a quick, sharp sound, like a lid snapping shut.
Think of something else, then test: how do you feel about the food now?

entries.safety: Never with an eating disorder. Choose a food you do not need for health.

source.name: Richard Bandler · Joseph Cautela, covert sensitisation

words.meaning: Copying the details of one mind picture onto another.

entries.title: The Fast Phobia Cure (V-K Dissociation)
entries.what: Watching a frightening memory like an old film from far away, so the fear gets smaller.
entries.gives: Distance makes the fear smaller while you look at the memory.
entries.pic: A cinema: the screen, the seat, and you watching from the back room.

steps.t: Imagine sitting in a cinema.
Float to the back room, where the projector is.
From there, watch yourself in the seat, watching the screen.
On the screen: a black and white picture of the moment before the memory.
Play the film quickly to the moment after, when you were safe.
Then play it backwards, very fast, in colour.
Repeat 3 to 5 times.
Think of it gently. Notice the difference.

entries.safety: Not a substitute for phobia or trauma treatment. Work with a qualified clinician.

source.name: Richard Bandler · later the RTM protocol

words.meaning: A strong fear of something specific, such as spiders.
Watching yourself watching yourself. It makes the memory feel far away.

entries.title: Surface Structure & Deep Structure
entries.what: Spoken words are a short version of a much fuller inner experience.
entries.gives: You know that words leave things out, so you ask about the rest.
entries.pic: An iceberg: the words above the water, the full experience below.

steps.t: Hear a sentence, such as 'Work is hard.'
Notice: this is the surface structure, the short version.
Ask what is underneath: who, what, when, how?
Each answer brings back part of the deep structure, the full experience.
Use the Meta Model to ask these questions in a structured way.

words.meaning: The words a person actually says.
The full experience behind the words.

entries.title: The Meta Model
entries.what: Questions that fill in what a person's words leave out.
entries.gives: A vague problem becomes clear, and a clear problem can be solved.
entries.pic: A magnifying glass over words: looking for what is missing.

steps.t: Listen to the exact sentence.
'They never listen.' Ask: 'Who exactly? Never?'
'I always fail.' Ask: 'Always? Was there a time you didn't?'
'I can't.' Ask: 'What would happen if you did?'
'He's angry with me.' Ask: 'How do you know?'
'She makes me feel small.' Ask: 'What exactly does she do?'
Ask one question at a time, kindly.

source.name: Bandler & Grinder 1975, modelled on Virginia Satir and Fritz Perls

words.meaning: Turning one bad moment into 'always' or 'never'.
Believing you know what someone feels without asking.

entries.title: The Milton Model
entries.what: Calm, general language that lets the listener fill in their own meaning.
entries.gives: People relax and find their own answers instead of resisting yours.
entries.pic: A soft cloud: words that are open, not sharp.

steps.t: Start with what is true right now: 'You're sitting here, breathing, listening.'
Use open words people fill in themselves: 'a change', 'something new'.
Offer two choices that both move forward: 'Today or tomorrow?'
Ask soft questions: 'Can you take a deep breath?'
Link gently: 'As you breathe out, you can relax.'
Speak slowly and calmly, with pauses.
Use it only to help the listener.

entries.time: Daily practice, 2 or 3 patterns at a time

source.name: Bandler & Grinder 1975, modelled on Milton H. Erickson

words.meaning: Words general enough that each person fills in their own meaning, like 'a change'.

entries.title: Chunking (Up, Down & Lateral)
entries.what: Moving a conversation up to the big picture, down to the details, or across to another example.
entries.gives: People agree on the big picture and get clear on the details.
entries.pic: A ladder: up for the big picture, down for the details.

steps.t: Ask yourself: are we talking big picture or details?
Go up: 'What is this for?'
Go down: 'What exactly?'
Go across: 'What is another example?'
In an argument, go up until you both agree.
Then go down to the next small step.

words.meaning: A piece of an idea. Big chunks are the big picture; small chunks are details.

entries.title: Clean Language
entries.what: Simple questions that look into a person's own words and images without adding yours.
entries.gives: The person finds their own answer, untouched by your ideas.
entries.pic: A speech bubble with an empty frame: nothing added by the listener.

steps.t: Listen for the person's own words and images, such as 'I feel stuck.'
Repeat their words exactly.
Ask: 'And what kind of stuck is that stuck?'
Ask: 'And is there anything else about that stuck?'
Ask: 'And where is that stuck?'
Ask: 'And what would you like to have happen?'
Never add your own words or ideas.

source.name: David Grove · James Lawley & Penny Tompkins, 2000

words.meaning: A question that uses only the person's own words.
An image that stands for something, such as 'stuck'.

entries.title: Isomorphic Metaphors
entries.what: A story with the same shape as the listener's problem, and a good ending.
entries.gives: People find the answer themselves inside the story, and remember it.
entries.pic: An open book: the story carries the message.

steps.t: What is the person's problem?
What do they want instead?
What do they need to understand?
Think of a world they love: sport, cooking, cars.
Make a story in that world with the same problem and a good ending.
Tell the story.
Do not explain it. Let them find the meaning.

source.name: David Gordon, 1978, after Milton H. Erickson

words.meaning: A story that stands for something else.

entries.title: Nested Loops
entries.what: Telling stories inside stories, then finishing them in reverse order.
entries.gives: Unfinished stories hold attention, so the message in the middle is heard.
entries.pic: Three arcs, one inside another: story A, story B, story C.

steps.t: Choose the message.
Start story A. Stop at an exciting point.
Start story B. Stop at an exciting point.
Tell story C, with the message inside it.
Finish story C.
Finish story B.
Finish story A.

words.meaning: A story you start but have not finished yet. The mind wants to hear the end.

entries.title: Core NLP Frames
entries.what: Six standard frames that guide a conversation: outcome, ecology, evidence, as if, contrast and relevancy.
entries.gives: Each frame keeps a talk focused in a different way.
entries.pic: Six frames in two rows: six ways of focusing a talk.

steps.t: Learn the six frames, then use them in conversation.
Outcome frame: 'What do you want?'
Ecology frame: 'Is this good for you and for others?'
Evidence frame: 'How will you know you have it?'
As-if frame: 'Imagine it is done. What did you do?'
Contrast frame: 'What is different between when it works and when it doesn't?'
Relevancy frame: 'How does this connect to our goal?'
Choose the frame that fits the moment.

words.meaning: The focus that shapes how a situation is seen.

entries.title: As-If Frame
entries.what: Imagining the goal is already done, then asking how you did it.
entries.gives: It gets you past 'I don't know' and 'I can't'.
entries.pic: You now, and the future you who already did it.

steps.t: Hear the block: 'I don't know' or 'I can't.'
Ask: 'If you did know, what would you say?'
Or: 'It is a year from now and it worked. What did you do?'
Let the answer come from that future place.
Write down the steps.
Come back to now and choose the first step.

words.meaning: Pretending something is already true, to see what you would do.

entries.title: Contrast Frame
entries.what: Comparing a time it works with a time it doesn't, to find the key difference.
entries.gives: The difference shows you exactly what to change.
entries.pic: Two boxes, almost the same: find the one difference.

steps.t: Pick a time it worked and a time it didn't.
Describe each one in detail.
List what was the same.
List what was different.
Pick the difference that matters most.
Bring that into the time that doesn't work.

words.meaning: The one change that makes the biggest difference.

entries.title: Relevancy Frame
entries.what: Asking how a point connects to the goal of the meeting.
entries.gives: Meetings stay on track without arguments.
entries.pic: An arrow to a target, with a dotted line drifting away.

steps.t: Agree the goal at the start.
Write it where everyone can see it.
When the talk drifts, ask: 'How does this help our goal?'
If it helps, continue.
If not, save it for later.
Return to the goal.

words.meaning: Connected to what we are trying to do.

entries.title: Pre-Framing & Post-Framing
entries.what: Setting the meaning before something happens, and confirming it after.
entries.gives: People know what to expect, and leave with the right meaning.
entries.pic: Two brackets around an event: one before, one after.

steps.t: Before: decide the meaning you want people to take away.
Pre-frame: 'In the next ten minutes we'll do a simple exercise. Some parts may feel unusual, and that is normal.'
Do the activity.
Post-frame: 'Notice what changed. That is what this exercise is for.'
Ask what they will take away.

words.meaning: Setting expectations before an event.
Fixing the meaning right after an event.

entries.title: Context Reframing
entries.what: Finding a place where a 'too much' trait is actually a strength.
entries.gives: Most traits are useful somewhere.
entries.pic: The same circle in two boxes: grey in one place, bronze in the other.

steps.t: Listen for 'I'm too…' or 'She's too…'.
Ask: 'Where would this be useful?'
Find one clear example.
Example: 'too stubborn' becomes 'strong enough to say no to pressure'.
Say it as a question.
Let the person think about it in their own time.

words.meaning: The place or situation. The same trait can be a problem in one place and a strength in another.

entries.title: Content (Meaning) Reframing
entries.what: Finding another meaning for the same event.
entries.gives: When the meaning changes, the feeling changes.
entries.pic: A frame with a turning arrow: same picture, new way of seeing it.

steps.t: Write down the complaint in the person's own words.
Ask: 'What else could this mean?'
Look for the good reason behind the behaviour.
Offer it softly: 'Is it possible that…?'
Example: 'He's too controlling' becomes 'He wants to protect you.'
Watch their face and breathing relax.
Never say their feeling is wrong.

source.name: Bandler & Grinder, Reframing, 1982 · James Gross, cognitive reappraisal

words.meaning: Seeing the same thing in a new way. Like turning a photo to see it from another side.

entries.title: The Six-Step Reframe
entries.what: Finding what a habit gives you, and finding better ways to get it.
entries.gives: A habit stays until its need is met another way.
entries.pic: Six steps up: six small steps to a better choice.

steps.t: Name the habit you want to change.
Ask the part of you behind it for a yes or no signal, such as a warm feeling.
Ask it: 'What do you want for me?' For example: rest or comfort.
Find three new ways to get the same thing.
Ask that part: 'Will you use these instead?'
Check: does any other part of you object? If yes, repeat with that part.

entries.safety: For addiction, work with specialist support.

words.meaning: A side of you that wants something, as in 'part of me wants to rest'.
Every habit, even a bad one, is trying to give you something good.

entries.title: Perceptual Positions (1st, 2nd & 3rd)
entries.what: Looking at a situation from three places: you, the other person, and an observer.
entries.gives: You see the whole picture, not only your side.
entries.pic: You, the other person, and an observer above.

steps.t: Choose a situation with one other person.
Place 1, you: see it through your own eyes. What do you want?
Step to the side and shake it off.
Place 2, them: stand where they stand. See it through their eyes.
Step to the side again.
Place 3, observer: watch both of you from a calm distance.
What does the observer notice?
Return to place 1 with what you learned.

source.name: John Grinder & Judith DeLozier · Robert Dilts

words.meaning: The place you look from: me, you, or an outside observer.

entries.title: 4th Position (Systemic Perspective)
entries.what: Seeing a relationship or team as one whole system.
entries.gives: You see what the whole needs, not only each person.
entries.pic: Three people inside one large circle: the whole system.

steps.t: First, take 1st, 2nd and 3rd position, as in Perceptual Positions.
Now step into 4th position: the 'we' of the whole relationship or team.
Ask: 'What does this whole system need?'
Ask: 'What would be best for all of us?'
Bring that answer back to 1st position.

words.meaning: A group of parts that affect each other, such as a family or a team.
The view from the whole group: 'we'.

entries.title: The Meta-Mirror
entries.what: Solving a conflict by seeing it from four places, including coaching yourself.
entries.gives: Seeing yourself from outside shows you new choices.
entries.pic: Four people: you, them, an observer, and a coach watching it all.

steps.t: Place 1: you, facing the other person.
Place 2: stand in their place.
Place 3: watch both of you from a distance.
Place 4: watch it all. Ask: what does the 'me' in place 1 need?
Give that to yourself: calm, patience or courage.
Return to place 1. Notice what has changed.

words.meaning: A place one step above everything, where you can guide yourself.

entries.title: Parts Integration (Visual Squash)
entries.what: Helping two sides of you that want different things to work together.
entries.gives: Self-sabotage often comes from two parts that want the same good thing in different ways.
entries.pic: Two open hands moving towards each other.

steps.t: Name the conflict: 'Part of me wants…, and part of me keeps…'
Hold both hands out, palms up. Close your eyes.
Imagine the part that holds you back on one hand. Give it a name.
Imagine the part that wants the goal on the other hand.
Ask the first part: 'What do you want for me?' Keep asking: 'And what will that give me?'
Do the same with the second part, until both want the same thing.
Let each part give the other something useful.
Let your hands come together on their own. Bring them to your chest.

entries.safety: Not for dissociative conditions or trauma. Work with a qualified clinician.

words.meaning: When part of you wants one thing and part of you wants another.
Getting in your own way, such as putting off what you want most.

entries.title: The T.O.T.E. Model
entries.what: The basic loop behind every action: Test, Operate, Test, Exit.
entries.gives: It shows how any habit or skill works, step by step.
entries.pic: A loop: test, act, test again, then exit at the top.

steps.t: Choose a simple task, such as making tea.
Test: is the water hot? No.
Operate: heat the water.
Test again: is it hot now? Yes.
Exit: move on to the next step.
Notice this loop in your own habits.

words.meaning: Test, Operate, Test, Exit.
A cycle that checks, acts and checks again.

entries.title: Strategy Notation (VAKOG Sequencing)
entries.what: Writing a mental strategy as a short code of senses.
entries.gives: You can see, compare and change a strategy on paper.
entries.pic: Letters and arrows: see outside, talk inside, feel inside.

steps.t: Learn the code: V seeing, A hearing, K feeling, Ad self-talk, O smell, G taste.
Add a small 'e' for outside (external) and 'i' for inside (internal).
Example: you see a cake (Ve), you say 'I want that' (Ad), you feel desire (Ki).
Write it as: Ve → Ad → Ki.
Write one of your own habits in this code.
Mark the step you would like to change.

words.meaning: Something outside you, such as a sight in the room.
Something inside you, such as a picture in your mind.

entries.title: Strategy Elicitation
entries.what: Finding the exact steps a person follows to do something well.
entries.gives: Once you can see the steps, you can copy or improve them.
entries.pic: Check, act, check again: the loop every task follows.

steps.t: Ask about a time they did the task well.
Ask: 'What was the very first thing?'
Ask: 'And then what?' until the end.
Write each step: did they see, hear, feel or say something?
Mark how they knew to continue or to stop.
Find the step that fails, and put a better one there.

words.meaning: Test, Operate, Test, Exit: check, act, check again, finish.

entries.title: Strategy Utilisation & Installation
entries.what: Using, improving or installing a strategy that works.
entries.gives: You copy what works and replace what does not.
entries.pic: A row of blocks with one block replaced.

steps.t: Elicit the current strategy, step by step.
Elicit a strategy that works, from yourself or someone else.
Utilise: present information in the order the person's strategy expects.
Improve: change or reorder the step that fails.
Install: rehearse the new sequence many times.
Anchor each step so it runs smoothly.
Test it in a real situation, and future pace.

words.meaning: Use a person's own strategy to communicate with them.
Practise a new strategy until it runs by itself.

entries.title: New Behaviour Generator
entries.what: A step-by-step way to practise a new behaviour in your mind.
entries.gives: When you have practised it inside, it is ready outside.
entries.pic: A screen with you on it, practising.

steps.t: Choose the new behaviour and where you want it.
Ask: 'If I could do this, what would it look like?'
Watch yourself doing it, as if on a screen.
Adjust until it looks right.
Step into the picture and do it from inside.
If anything feels wrong, step out and adjust.
Imagine using it in a future situation.

words.meaning: What you do.

entries.title: Direction Filter: Towards & Away From
entries.what: Some people move towards goals; others move away from problems.
entries.gives: You motivate each person in the direction that moves them.
entries.pic: A dot with one arrow towards a target and one away from a problem.

steps.t: Ask: 'What do you want in your work?'
Listen: 'I want growth' is towards. 'I don't want stress' is away from.
Ask a second question to check.
For towards people, talk about gains and goals.
For away-from people, talk about problems avoided.
Notice your own filter.

source.name: Leslie Cameron-Bandler · Rodger Bailey, LAB Profile · Shelle Rose Charvet, 1995

words.meaning: Motivated by what you want.
Motivated by what you want to avoid.

entries.title: Reference Filter: Internal & External
entries.what: Some people judge by their own sense; others need feedback from others.
entries.gives: You give feedback in the way each person can take it in.
entries.pic: A person with an inner circle, and arrows of feedback from outside.

steps.t: Ask: 'How do you know you did a good job?'
Listen: 'I just know' is internal. 'Others tell me' is external.
For internal people: give information and let them decide.
For external people: give clear feedback and facts.
Notice your own filter.

source.name: Leslie Cameron-Bandler · Rodger Bailey, LAB Profile · Shelle Rose Charvet, 1995

words.meaning: Deciding by your own standards.
Deciding by feedback from others.

entries.title: Action Filter: Proactive & Reactive
entries.what: Some people act at once; others wait, think and analyse first.
entries.gives: You plan work and messages that fit how a person starts.
entries.pic: One arrow straight ahead, one line pausing at a dot.

steps.t: Listen to how a person describes starting something.
Short, active sentences, such as 'Just do it', suggest proactive.
Long, careful sentences, such as 'Let's think it through', suggest reactive.
For proactive people: 'Go ahead and get it done.'
For reactive people: 'Take time to consider this.'
Most people mix both. Notice which one leads.

source.name: Leslie Cameron-Bandler · Rodger Bailey, LAB Profile · Shelle Rose Charvet, 1995

words.meaning: Starts quickly.
Waits, thinks and then responds.

entries.title: Chunk Size Filter: Global & Specific
entries.what: Some people think in the big picture; others think in details.
entries.gives: You explain at the level a person can follow.
entries.pic: One big block next to many small blocks.

steps.t: Ask: 'Tell me about your last project.'
Listen: a short overview suggests global; many steps and details suggest specific.
For global people: start with the big picture.
For specific people: give the steps in order.
In a mixed group: overview first, then details.
Notice your own filter.

source.name: Leslie Cameron-Bandler · Rodger Bailey, LAB Profile · Shelle Rose Charvet, 1995

words.meaning: Big picture.
Details, step by step.

entries.title: Relationship Filter: Sameness & Difference
entries.what: Some people notice what is the same; others notice what is different.
entries.gives: You present change in a way each person accepts.
entries.pic: Two matching squares, and one different shape.

steps.t: Ask: 'What is the relationship between your work this year and last year?'
'It's the same' suggests sameness.
'It's completely different' suggests difference.
'The same, but better' suggests sameness with exception.
For sameness people: stress what stays the same. For difference people: stress what is new.
Notice your own filter.

source.name: Leslie Cameron-Bandler · Rodger Bailey, LAB Profile · Shelle Rose Charvet, 1995

words.meaning: Noticing what matches.
Noticing what is new or changed.

entries.title: Reason Filter: Options & Procedures
entries.what: Some people want choices; others want a clear step-by-step process.
entries.gives: You give each person instructions in the form they follow best.
entries.pic: Branching paths above, one path of steps below.

steps.t: Ask: 'Why did you choose your current job?'
Options people list reasons and possibilities.
Procedures people tell how it happened, step by step.
For options people: offer choices.
For procedures people: give the right steps, in order.
Notice your own filter.

source.name: Leslie Cameron-Bandler · Rodger Bailey, LAB Profile · Shelle Rose Charvet, 1995

words.meaning: Wanting choices and flexibility.
Wanting a proven sequence of steps.

entries.title: Convincer Channel & Mode
entries.what: Finding how a person becomes convinced: through which sense, and how often.
entries.gives: You give proof in the way the person actually decides.
entries.pic: A tick and three dots: how many times before they are sure.

steps.t: Ask: 'How do you know someone is good at their job?'
Channel: do they need to see it, hear it, read it or do it with them?
Ask: 'How often must they show it before you are convinced?'
Mode: automatically, a number of times, over a period of time, or consistently every time.
Give proof in their channel and mode.
Respect a no.

words.meaning: The sense used to gather proof: see, hear, read or do.
How often proof is needed: automatic, number of times, period of time, consistent.

entries.title: Dilts' Neurological Levels (Logical Levels)
entries.what: Six levels of who you are, from where you are to who you are.
entries.gives: A change at a higher level changes everything below it.
entries.pic: Six stacked levels: environment, behaviour, capabilities, beliefs and values, identity, purpose.

steps.t: Choose a hard situation. Mark six spots in a line on the floor.
Spot 1, Where: the place, the time, who is there.
Step back to spot 2, What: what you do there.
Spot 3, How: the skills you use.
Spot 4, Why: what matters to you.
Spot 5, Who: who you are. Find a symbol for it.
Spot 6, Purpose: what larger whole you are part of, and what you serve beyond yourself.
Walk forward through every spot, taking the symbol with you.
Back at the situation, notice what has changed.

words.meaning: Robert Dilts' six levels: environment, behaviour, capabilities, beliefs and values, identity, purpose.
Who you are, not only what you do.

entries.title: Values Elicitation & Hierarchy
entries.what: Finding what matters most to you, in order.
entries.gives: Your choices get easier when you know your order.
entries.pic: Bars from longest to shortest: the most important at the top.

steps.t: Choose one area of life, such as work.
Ask: 'What is important to me about work?'
Keep asking 'What else?' until nothing comes.
Choose the most important. Then the next.
Number the list.
Test: 'If I had everything except number one, would I be happy?'
Use the list to make choices.

words.meaning: What matters most to you, such as freedom, family or health.

entries.title: Values Conflict Resolution & Alignment
entries.what: Resolving the friction when two important values pull against each other.
entries.gives: You stop feeling torn, and decide with clarity.
entries.pic: Two arrows pulling apart, then one arrow in a single direction.

steps.t: Name the two values, such as freedom and security.
For each one, ask: 'What will this give me?' Keep asking.
Find the higher value both serve, such as peace of mind.
Find a way to meet both values in your life.
Reorder your values if needed.
Check: does the friction feel smaller now?

words.meaning: When two things that matter to you seem to exclude each other.

entries.title: Complex Equivalence & Cause-Effect Mapping
entries.what: Finding the hidden rules that link an event to a meaning: 'X means Y' and 'X causes Y'.
entries.gives: When you can see the rule, you can question it.
entries.pic: X equals Y: the hidden rule made visible.

steps.t: Listen for 'means': 'He's late, so he doesn't care.'
Listen for 'makes' or 'because': 'You make me angry.'
Write the rule: late = doesn't care.
Ask: 'How does being late mean not caring?'
Ask: 'Has anyone been late and still cared?'
Ask: 'How exactly does what they do cause your feeling?'
Write a new, more accurate rule.

words.meaning: Treating two different things as the same: X means Y.
Believing one thing makes another happen: X causes Y.

entries.title: Submodality Belief Change
entries.what: Changing a belief that holds you back, so it feels like something you used to believe.
entries.gives: It is easier to put a belief away than to fight it.
entries.pic: A cabinet of drawers: the old belief goes into the drawer of old beliefs.

steps.t: Name the belief, such as 'I'm not good enough.'
Check that you are ready, and that no part of you objects.
Notice how the belief looks in your mind: where it is, how big.
Think of something you used to believe, like 'I am seven years old.' Notice where it is.
Move the old belief to that same place. Make it look the same.
Think of something you are sure of, like 'The sun will rise tomorrow.' Notice where it is.
