Choose your new belief. Put it in that same place, with the same look.
Ask: 'Do I still believe the old one? Yes or no?'

entries.safety: If a belief is part of depression, work with a qualified clinician.

words.meaning: A belief that stops you, such as 'I can't'.

entries.title: Sleight of Mouth Patterns
entries.what: Questions that loosen a belief that holds someone back.
entries.gives: A belief seen from many sides loses its grip.
entries.pic: One sentence, many arrows: looking at a belief from different sides.

steps.t: Hear the belief, such as 'Failing means I'm useless.'
New meaning: 'Or does failing mean you are learning?'
Result: 'If you keep that belief, where will it lead?'
Exception: 'Has anyone failed and still done well?'
Purpose: 'What is this belief trying to protect you from?'
Ask one question at a time, warmly.

words.meaning: Something you think is true, such as 'I'm bad at maths'.
Robert Dilts' 14 conversational patterns, such as intention, redefine, consequence and counter-example.

entries.title: Core Transformation
entries.what: Following a behaviour back to the deep state it is reaching for, such as peace.
entries.gives: The deep state becomes available directly, and the behaviour can change.
entries.pic: Circles inside circles, with a core at the centre.

steps.t: Choose a behaviour or feeling you want to change.
Ask the part behind it: 'What do you want?'
Ask: 'If you have that fully, what do you want through having it that is even more important?'
Repeat until you reach a core state, such as peace, wholeness or presence.
Step into that core state and feel it fully.
Let the core state flow back through each step, to the behaviour.
Notice how the original behaviour feels now.

words.meaning: A deep state of being, such as peace or wholeness.
A side of you with its own aim.

entries.title: Timeline Elicitation
entries.what: Finding how you arrange past, present and future in space in your mind.
entries.gives: It shows how you relate to time, and is the base for all timeline work.
entries.pic: Left: a time line through the body. Right: a time line in front of the body.

steps.t: Ask: 'If you point to your past, where is it?'
Ask: 'Where is your future?'
Ask: 'Where is now?'
If the line passes through your body, that is 'In Time'.
If the whole line lies in front of you, that is 'Through Time'.
Notice how this matches the way you plan and keep time.

words.meaning: The time line passes through you: you live in the moment.
The time line is in front of you: you see the whole plan.

entries.title: Releasing Root Negative Emotions
entries.what: Releasing an old negative emotion by going above your timeline to before the first event that caused it.
entries.gives: When you keep the learning from the past, the emotion can be released.
entries.pic: An eye high above a line of time, looking down at the first event.

steps.t: Choose one emotion. The standard order is anger, sadness, fear, hurt, guilt. Start with anger.
Check that you are ready, and that it is right to let it go.
Float high above your timeline.
Go back to just before the first event connected to this emotion.
Stay above it and before it. Never step into the event.
Ask: 'What can I learn from this, so I can let the emotion go?'
Keep the learning. Notice the emotion is gone from this point.
Float back to now along the timeline.
Check later memories. Then repeat with the next emotion in the order.

entries.safety: Not for trauma, PTSD or depression. Stop at any time; work with a qualified clinician.

source.name: Tad James & Wyatt Woodsmall, Time Line Therapy, 1988

words.meaning: The first event connected to a feeling.
The standard order in Time Line Therapy: anger, sadness, fear, hurt, guilt.

entries.title: Clearing Limiting Decisions
entries.what: Finding an early decision, such as 'I'm not good enough', and letting it go from above the timeline.
entries.gives: An old conclusion stops running your life.
entries.pic: A line of time, seen from above, with the first decision crossed out.

steps.t: Name the limiting decision.
Ask: 'When was the first time I made this decision?' Trust the first answer.
Float above your timeline, high and safe.
Go back to just before that first event.
Look at the event from above. Ask: 'What can I learn here?'
Keep the learning. Let the decision go.
Float back to now along the timeline, noticing later events change.
Check: can you still find the old decision as strongly?

entries.safety: Not for trauma or depression. Work with a qualified clinician.

words.meaning: A conclusion made early in life that still limits you.

entries.title: Re-Imprinting
entries.what: Bringing adult resources to an early experience that shaped a belief.
entries.gives: The belief formed back then can be updated with what you know now.
entries.pic: A small figure and a large figure, with a resource passed between them.

steps.t: Name a limiting belief and the feeling that goes with it.
Follow the feeling back to an early memory where it formed.
Step out of the memory and watch it from outside.
Ask: what did each person there need?
Give each person in the memory the resource they needed.
Step into each person's place and feel it with the resource.
Step into your younger self and receive the resources.
Come back to now. Notice how the belief has changed.

entries.safety: Not for trauma or abuse memories. Work with a qualified clinician.

words.meaning: An early experience that shaped a belief.
What was needed then: safety, courage, understanding.

entries.title: Installing Compelling Futures
entries.what: Placing one clear goal on a date in your imagined future.
entries.gives: A goal with a date and a clear picture feels real and close.
entries.pic: A line of time from today to the future, with a flag on your goal date.

steps.t: Choose one goal with a clear date.
Picture the moment it is done: what you see, hear and feel.
Make the picture bright, clear and close.
Imagine your life as a line: the past behind you, the future in front.
In your mind, carry the picture forward to the date and place it there.
See the steps between today and that date.
Come back to today and take the first step.

source.name: Tad James, time line goal setting

words.meaning: Your life imagined as a line: yesterday behind you, tomorrow in front.

entries.title: NLP Modelling Methodology
entries.what: The five stages of copying excellence from one person and teaching it to others.
entries.gives: This is how NLP itself was created.
entries.pic: Five rising steps: copy, map, test, simplify, teach.

steps.t: Choose an excellent person and one skill.
Stage 1, Implicit modelling: copy them without analysing, until you get similar results.
Stage 2, Explicit modelling: map their beliefs, strategies and physiology.
Stage 3, Testing: remove one element at a time; keep what changes the result.
Stage 4, Simplification: reduce the model to what is essential.
Stage 5, Transfer: teach it to others.
Compare their results with the expert's.

words.meaning: Studying and copying how someone gets an excellent result.
Learned by doing, without explaining.

entries.title: What the Science Says
entries.what: What research says about NLP, in plain words.
entries.gives: You know what is proven and what is not, so you use the tools honestly.
entries.pic: A balance: what is proven on one side, what is not on the other.

steps.t: Most scientists say the theory behind NLP is not proven.
Some claims were tested and failed, such as reading thoughts from eye movements.
Some tools match methods that are proven.
Seeing an event in a new way works. Therapists use this every day.
Looking at a bad memory from a distance makes it feel smaller.
Practising in your mind first helps you do it for real.
Use NLP for coaching and conversation, never as medical treatment.
For trauma, depression, addiction or eating problems, see a qualified professional.

source.name: Sturt et al. 2012 · Witkowski 2010 · Wiseman et al. 2012

words.meaning: Tested many times by researchers, with the same result each time.
Something that sounds scientific but did not pass the tests.

entries.title: PAW Process
entries.what: Three quick questions to test a goal: is it possible, can I do it, is it worth it?
entries.gives: You find the weak point of a goal before you start.
entries.pic: Three boxes to tick: Possible, Able, Worth it.

steps.t: Write your goal in one sentence.
Possible: has anyone done this, or something like it?
Able: can you do it, or learn how?
Worth it: is it worth the time, money and effort?
Give each a score from 0 to 10.
Work on the lowest score first, or change the goal.

words.meaning: Possible, Able, Worth it.

entries.title: Congruence Check
entries.what: Checking that all of you agrees with a new choice.
entries.gives: If part of you says no, it will block the change later.
entries.pic: A person and a tick: words, body and feeling all say yes.

steps.t: Think of the new choice.
Ask yourself: does any part of me say no?
Notice any doubt, tight feeling or small inner voice.
If there is one, ask: what does this part want for me?
Add that need to your plan.
Ask again until you feel a clear yes.

words.meaning: When your words, your body and your feelings all agree.

entries.title: First- & Second-Order Change
entries.what: Two kinds of change: fixing one habit, or changing what causes many habits.
entries.gives: You see whether a small fix is enough or a deeper change is needed.
entries.pic: A small box inside a big box: one habit inside a bigger pattern.

steps.t: Name the problem.
Small change: change one habit in one place.
Watch: does the problem come back in another form?
If yes, look deeper: what belief or rule sits behind it?
Change that belief or rule.
Check whether many things change at once.

source.name: Paul Watzlawick, John Weakland & Richard Fisch, 1974 · Gregory Bateson

words.meaning: A small fix: one habit in one place. Like fixing one leak.
A deeper fix: the cause of many habits. Like replacing old pipes.

entries.title: Recursive Change Architecture
entries.what: A plan to make a change last.
entries.gives: A change you test again and again stays.
entries.pic: A circle of arrows: test, and test again.

steps.t: Make the change with one tool.
Test it right away.
Imagine it in three different places.
Check that it is good for your whole life.
Test again after a day, a week and a month.
If the old habit returns, go one level deeper.

words.meaning: Checking a change again, later.

entries.title: Four Frames
entries.what: Four simple sentence starters that keep a conversation positive.
entries.gives: How you frame a talk decides where it goes.
entries.pic: Four frames: four ways of looking at the same talk.

steps.t: Choose one frame to practise this week.
Agreement: say 'I agree, and…' instead of 'I understand, but…'.
Purpose: ask 'What is this for?'
What if: ask 'What would happen if you did?'
Positive: turn 'I don't want X' into 'What do you want instead?'
Use it until it feels natural, then add the next.

source.name: NLP frames · Tversky & Kahneman 1981, framing effect

words.meaning: The way a situation is presented. Like a picture frame, it changes how you see what is inside.

entries.title: Love Strategies
entries.what: Finding out how a person knows they are loved: what they need to see, hear or feel.
entries.gives: Love given their way is love they notice.
entries.pic: A heart.

steps.t: Ask: 'How do you know someone loves you?'
Listen: is it something they see, hear or feel?
Ask about one time they felt very loved.
Find the exact sign: a look, words or a touch.
Share your own answer.
Give love through their sign, often.

words.meaning: The sign that tells a person they are loved. For one it is a hug, for another kind words.

entries.title: Family Therapy Model
entries.what: A way to calm repeated fights in a couple or a family.
entries.gives: Most family fights are about how, not about love.
entries.pic: Two adults and a child.

steps.t: Each person says what they want for the family.
Find the aim everyone shares, such as 'a calm home'.
List the looks, words or tones that start fights.
Agree a new signal to use instead of each one.
Share how each person knows they are loved.
Each person agrees to one change.
Check together in two weeks.

entries.safety: For abuse or high conflict, work with a qualified family therapist.

source.name: Virginia Satir, modelled by Bandler & Grinder

words.meaning: Something small, like a look or a word, that starts a big reaction.

entries.title: Meta Model III
entries.what: Six short questions that find the cause of a problem.
entries.gives: You reach the real problem fast.
entries.pic: A target with a magnifying glass: finding the exact point.

steps.t: 'What exactly is the problem?'
'How do you know it is a problem?'
'When does it happen, and when does it not?'
'What happens just before it starts?'
'What do you want instead?'
'What stops you having that now?'
Choose the tool that fits the answer.

source.name: NLP trainers, after the Meta Model of Bandler & Grinder

words.meaning: What makes the problem start.

entries.title: Negotiation Frame
entries.what: Looking past what each side demands to what each side needs.
entries.gives: When you find the shared need, both sides can win.
entries.pic: Two arrows meeting at the top: both sides reach the same aim.

steps.t: Hear each side's demand.
Ask each side: 'What is that for?'
Keep asking until both share one aim.
Think of several options that serve that aim.
Choose the fairest option together.
Agree who does what, and by when.

source.name: Roger Fisher & William Ury, 1981 · NLP chunking

words.meaning: What someone asks for.
Why they ask for it.

entries.title: Effective Meeting Pattern
entries.what: A simple structure for a short, clear meeting.
entries.gives: Less time wasted, more agreement.
entries.pic: A table with people around it.

steps.t: Decide the result you want before the meeting.
Agree how you will know you got it.
Start with the agenda, then remind everyone why you are meeting.
When the talk drifts, ask how it helps the goal.
If there is conflict, look at it from outside, like an observer.
End with actions: who, what, when.
Repeat the decisions out loud.

words.meaning: The list of topics for the meeting.

entries.title: Leverage Pattern
entries.what: Finding the one small change that moves everything else.
entries.gives: Small effort in the right place saves big effort everywhere.
entries.pic: A lever: a small push at the right point lifts a heavy weight.

steps.t: Write the chain: trigger, thought, feeling, action, result.
Ask: where would one small change shift the rest?
Test changing your words.
Test changing your posture or breathing.
Test changing your first thought.
Keep the change that works best.

words.meaning: The place where a little effort makes a big difference.

entries.title: Five-Step Sales Process
entries.what: Five honest steps for offering something to someone.
entries.gives: A sale that truly meets a person's needs is good for both sides.
entries.pic: Five arrows, one after another.

steps.t: Build trust first.
Ask open questions about what they need.
Find what matters most to them.
Show only how the offer truly meets that.
Ask for a clear decision.
If it doesn't fit, say so.
Never push, and never invent urgency.

words.meaning: A question that cannot be answered with yes or no.

entries.title: Affirmations & Incantations
entries.what: Saying a strong sentence out loud while your body matches it.
entries.gives: Words and body together change how you feel, quickly.
entries.pic: A person speaking out loud.

steps.t: Write one short sentence in the present, such as 'I am calm and ready.'
Stand tall. Breathe deeply.
Say it out loud, with full voice.
Add a movement that matches it.
Repeat for two minutes.
Use it before an important moment.

words.meaning: A sentence said out loud with feeling and movement, not only thought.

entries.title: Break State
entries.what: A quick surprise that stops a bad mood.
entries.gives: It clears your head before the next step.
entries.pic: A broken line: the old pattern stops.

steps.t: Notice the unhelpful mood.
Do something unexpected: stand up, clap, change rooms.
Or ask a random question: 'What did you have for breakfast?'
Take one deep breath.
Move straight on to the next task.

words.meaning: Anything that suddenly stops a habit or a mood.

entries.title: Physiology of Excellence
entries.what: Standing and breathing the way you do at your best.
entries.gives: An upright, open body helps you feel confident.
entries.pic: A person standing tall.

steps.t: Remember a time you were at your best.
Notice how you stood, breathed and spoke then.
Stand that way now.
Breathe that way.
Hold it for one minute.
Notice how you feel.
Use it before important moments.

words.meaning: Your body: posture, breathing, movement.

entries.title: Grounding
entries.what: Calming down by feeling your body and the floor.
entries.gives: It brings you back to now when you feel scattered.
entries.pic: A person with both feet on the ground.

steps.t: Sit or stand with your feet flat.
Soften your eyes and notice the edges of what you see.
Relax your jaw, shoulders and hands.
Name 3 things you see, 3 you hear, 3 you feel.
Breathe out longer than you breathe in, 3 times.
Feel your weight on the floor.

entries.safety: Breathe gently. Stop if you feel dizzy.

words.meaning: Bringing your attention back to your body and this moment.

entries.title: Godiva Chocolate Pattern
entries.what: Using the desire you feel for something you love to start a task you avoid.
entries.gives: You borrow motivation you already have.
entries.pic: A picture of what you love, with the task showing through its centre.

steps.t: Picture something you love very much.
Feel how strong the desire is.
Picture the task you avoid, small, behind it.
Make a small hole in the first picture so the task shows through.
Let the desire flow onto the task.
Clear the picture away.
Repeat 5 times, faster each time.

words.meaning: Letting the picture in your mind go blank, like turning off a TV.

entries.title: Neuro-Hypnotic Repatterning
entries.what: Linking learning and change with good feelings.
entries.gives: What feels good, you want to do again.
entries.pic: Calm waves and a small spark: a good feeling joined to learning.

steps.t: Sit comfortably. Breathe slowly.
Remember a time learning felt easy and fun.
Let that feeling grow.
Picture the new thing you want to learn.
Let the good feeling spread into it.
Repeat every day for a week.

entries.safety: Stop if distress appears.

words.meaning: Building a new habit of feeling.

entries.title: Change Personal History
entries.what: Taking a strong good feeling back into old memories of a bad one.
entries.gives: Old memories feel different when you bring help into them.
entries.pic: A line of time with dots: going back to old memories, with help.

steps.t: First, link a good feeling to one knuckle, as in Resource Anchor.
Name a small bad feeling that keeps coming back.
Remember the most recent time you felt it.
Press the knuckle while you remember.
Go to an earlier time. Keep pressing.
Notice how each memory feels different.
Imagine a future moment. Notice the new feeling.

entries.safety: Mild states only. For anxiety, depression or trauma, work with a qualified clinician.

words.meaning: Your past memories, and how they feel to you now.

entries.title: Mental Rehearsal
entries.what: Picturing yourself doing something well, step by step, before you do it.
entries.gives: Research shows practice in the mind improves real performance.
entries.pic: You, a dotted path, and the finish.

steps.t: Choose one skill or event.
Relax and close your eyes.
See it through your own eyes, at real speed.
Add the sounds and body feelings.
Go from the start to a good finish.
Repeat 3 times, every day.
Plan for one obstacle: 'If ___ happens, I will ___.'

words.meaning: Practising in your mind, the way athletes do.
Deciding now what you will do when a problem shows up.

entries.title: Eye Movement Integrator
entries.what: Moving your eyes slowly in different directions while you think of a mild memory.
entries.gives: It can loosen a stuck reaction to a small memory.
entries.pic: An eye following a looping path.

steps.t: Think of a mildly unpleasant memory. Score it from 0 to 10.
Follow a finger with your eyes: side to side, up and down, corner to corner.
Go slowly. Pause where the feeling changes, and breathe.
Continue for one to two minutes.
Score the memory again.
Repeat once if needed.

entries.safety: Mild memories only; stop if dizzy. For trauma, work with a qualified clinician.

words.meaning: When a memory stops feeling sharp and starts feeling like the past.

entries.title: New Orleans Flexibility Drill
entries.what: Practising many new reactions to the same old trigger.
entries.gives: The more choices you have, the weaker the old habit becomes.
entries.pic: One dot with many arrows: many ways to respond.

steps.t: Choose a trigger that always gets the same reaction from you.
Ask a friend to do the trigger.
React in a new way.
Repeat, with a different reaction each time.
Aim for ten different reactions.
Keep the three that work best.

words.meaning: Having more than one way to react.

entries.title: Tasking
entries.what: A real-life task you can only do with the new behaviour.
entries.gives: Doing it in real life proves the change.
entries.pic: A list with the first box ticked.

steps.t: Name the new behaviour.
Design a small task that needs it.
Choose a date.
Do the task.
Write down what happened.
Set the next task, a little bigger.

words.meaning: A real action you do to test a change.

entries.title: Motivation Strategies
entries.what: Changing how you get yourself started.
entries.gives: A kind inner voice gets you moving faster than a harsh one.
entries.pic: Steps going up, with an arrow.

steps.t: Remember a time you started something easily.
Notice what you saw, heard, told yourself and felt.
Remember a time you put something off. Notice the same things.
Compare the two.
Make your inner voice kind and clear.
Picture the task done, and how good it feels.
Make the first step tiny: five minutes.

words.meaning: How you talk to yourself in your head.

entries.title: Design Human Engineering
entries.what: Designing a brand-new way of thinking for a result you want.
entries.gives: Some goals need a way of thinking no one has shown you yet.
entries.pic: A grid with a rising line: a new plan, drawn step by step.

steps.t: Decide the result you want.
Decide how you will know you got it.
Design the steps in your mind: what to see, hear, say and feel, in order.
Practise the steps.
Test them in real life.
Improve one step at a time.

words.meaning: The order of steps your mind follows to get something done.

entries.title: Meta Programs
entries.what: Noticing the habits behind how a person makes decisions.
entries.gives: You can talk in the way a person decides.
entries.pic: A dot with two arrows: moving towards, or moving away.

steps.t: Ask: 'What do you want in a job?'
Listen: do they talk about what they want, or what they avoid?
Ask: 'How do you know you did well?'
Listen: do they just know inside, or do others tell them?
Notice the pattern.
Talk to them in the same way.

source.name: Leslie Cameron-Bandler · Rodger Bailey, LAB Profile

words.meaning: Moving to what you want.
Moving away from what you don't want.

entries.title: Ideal Self
entries.what: A clear picture of the best version of you, kept a little in front of you.
entries.gives: A picture you want to reach pulls you towards it.
entries.pic: You, glowing: your best self.

steps.t: Choose 3 to 5 qualities, such as calm, strong and kind.
Picture yourself with these qualities, seen from outside.
Keep the background empty: no specific place.
Keep the action open: no specific task.
Make the picture bigger, brighter and clearer.
Ask: does any part of me object? Add what it needs.
Picture this you in three future situations.

words.meaning: The best version of you, living what matters most to you.

entries.title: Genius Mapping
entries.what: Mapping how an excellent person thinks, feels and acts.
entries.gives: Excellence can be learned when you can see how it works.
entries.pic: You, and the expert you learn from.

steps.t: Choose an expert and one skill.
Watch them do it.
Ask what they believe about it.
Ask how they feel when they do it best.
Write down their steps.
Remove what makes no difference.
Practise what is left.

words.meaning: Studying how someone does something well, then copying it.

entries.title: Learning Strategies
entries.what: Learning in small pieces while you feel good.
entries.gives: Small pieces and a good mood make learning faster.
entries.pic: Small blocks building up.

steps.t: Remember a time learning was easy. Hold that feeling.
Cut the topic into small pieces.
Turn each piece into a picture or a drawing.
Say it out loud in your own words.
Use it right away in a small task.
Review it after a day and after a week.

words.meaning: Going over something again so you remember it.

entries.title: Spelling Strategy
entries.what: Spelling by picturing the word, not by sounding it out.
entries.gives: A clear picture of a word makes spelling easy.
entries.pic: Letters you see in your mind.

steps.t: Look at the word.
Look up and picture the word there.
Make the letters bright and clear.
Read the picture forwards, then backwards.
Write the word from the picture.
Check it against the real word.

words.meaning: Something you see with your eyes closed.

entries.title: Memory Pegs
entries.what: Remembering by placing pictures in places you know well.
entries.gives: Your mind finds pictures in familiar places easily.
entries.pic: A house with dots: each room holds one thing to remember.

steps.t: Choose ten places in your home, in order.
Learn the order: door, hall, kitchen…
Turn each thing to remember into a funny, clear picture.
Put each picture in one place.
To remember, walk through your home in your mind.
Go over it once more the same day.

source.name: Method of loci, Greek and Roman orators

words.meaning: A place you know well, used to store things you want to remember.

entries.title: Sorting Patterns
entries.what: Putting information into small groups so it is easy to remember.
entries.gives: Groups are easier to remember than long lists.
entries.pic: Three boxes with things sorted into them.

steps.t: Gather everything you need to remember.
Sort it into 3 to 5 groups.
Give each group a name.
Put the groups in a sensible order.
Remember the group names first, then what is inside.
Test yourself from memory.

words.meaning: Things that belong together.

entries.title: Digital Meter
entries.what: Adding numbers in your head by picturing a counter that rolls on.
entries.gives: The picture keeps count for you.
entries.pic: A counter showing numbers.

steps.t: Picture a digital counter showing zero.
Watch it roll to the first number.
Add the next number. Watch the digits roll on.
Let the numbers carry over by themselves.
Read the final number.
Practise with small numbers first.

words.meaning: A display that counts up, like a car's mileage.

entries.title: Visual Multiplication Chart
entries.what: Picturing a big times table so you can read the answers off it.
entries.gives: Seeing the answer is faster than reciting it.
entries.pic: A grid with one square marked: the answer.

steps.t: Look at a printed 10 by 10 times table.
Look up and picture it on a wall.
Colour one row at a time in your mind.
Find the answer where the row and the column meet.
Test yourself in random order.
Practise five minutes a day.

words.meaning: A grid of multiplication answers.

entries.title: Visualisation Development
entries.what: Exercises to see pictures in your mind more clearly.
entries.gives: Many tools here use mind pictures; practice makes them clearer.
entries.pic: A cube: a simple shape to practise picturing.

steps.t: Look at a simple object for ten seconds.
Close your eyes and picture it.
Open your eyes and compare.
Picture it again and change its colour.
Change its size, then how far away it is.
Practise every day with more detailed objects.

words.meaning: Make a picture in your mind.
